Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens,

We say that in this nation, “the power of government is derived from the consent of the governed.” We teach our children that the right to vote is the beating heart of our democracy. Yet today, millions of people who are citizens of this country—people who live under our laws, pay taxes, raise families, dream of a better future—are denied that fundamental right because they have been convicted of a felony.

Some have completed their sentences. Some are on parole or probation. Some are still behind bars.

I stand before you to say clearly and without apology: every citizen must have the right to vote—always. No exceptions, no fine print. Not “once you’ve done your time,” not “if a board approves,” not “if you can pay your fines.” Universal means universal. If you are a citizen, you have a voice.

We must restore voting rights to all citizens with felony convictions, including those who are currently incarcerated.

Why? Because a democracy that selectively silences its people is not a true democracy at all.

The core principle: the vote is not a reward

The right to vote is not a trophy to be earned by good behavior. It is not a coupon that the state can clip and reattach at will. It is not a privilege; it is a right.

We do not take away freedom of religion from those convicted of crimes. We do not strip them of their right to think, to speak, to hold beliefs. We do not say, “Because you were convicted, you may no longer be protected against cruel and unusual punishment.” Those rights are fundamental, whatever else a person has done.

Voting belongs in that same category.

When the state takes away the right to vote, it is not simply punishing an individual. It is redrawing the boundaries of the political community. It is saying: you still count when we tax you, when we police you, when we sentence you—but you do not count when we decide who holds power.

That is not justice. That is domination.

“They broke the social contract” – and then what?

People often say, “If you commit a serious crime, you’ve broken the social contract. Why should you help decide how society is run?”

I ask in return: when does that contract become unbreakable again?

If we claim prison is about rehabilitation, about accountability, about transformation, then we must also believe that people remain part of the community they have harmed. Responsibility requires relationship. You cannot ask someone to repair what they have broken and then exile them from the very process by which we decide how to build something better.

A person serving a sentence is still governed. They are governed intensely—by laws, prison policies, the decisions of legislators and executives and judges. To say they must obey these rules but cannot even cast a ballot about the people who make them is to practice pure, naked power, stripped of consent.

If the “social contract” means anything, it must mean this: as long as you are governed by the state, you are entitled to representation in that state.

Disenfranchisement as a tool of systemic racism and class control

Felony disenfranchisement in the United States did not emerge in a vacuum. It has roots. It has a purpose. And throughout our history, that purpose has often been to maintain racial hierarchy and suppress political power among the poor.

After the Civil War, when the Fifteenth Amendment barred states from denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude,” states found another way. They created and expanded felony disenfranchisement laws, then selectively enforced criminal statutes against Black citizens. They did not need to say the word “Black” in those laws. They only needed to design a system where, in practice, Black people would be convicted, imprisoned, and stripped of their political voice at disproportionate rates.

Today, the pattern endures.

People of color—and Black people in particular—are more likely to be arrested, more likely to be charged harshly, more likely to be convicted, and more likely to receive long sentences. That is not because they are more criminal. It is because our criminal legal system is steeped in bias, implicit and explicit.

Then, on top of a system that already treats people unequally, we layer a punishment that says: now you also lose your vote.

This is not neutral. This is not accidental. It is systemic disenfranchisement.

The result is predictable: in some communities, a staggering share of Black men cannot vote. In some states, entire neighborhoods are hollowed out politically. Their bodies remain; their voices are removed.

That is not public safety. That is political engineering.

Democracy cannot be conditional on perfection

If the right to vote is contingent on moral purity, then none of us should vote.

We all have fallen short. Some harms are punished by the criminal code; others are not. Which wrongs bring prison time—and which do not—often has less to do with morality and more to do with power, with race, with class, with whose wrongdoing is visible and whose wrongdoing is protected.

A banker who crashes an economy and ruins thousands of lives may never see a cell. A teenager who steals from a store may lose his freedom for years—and then lose his vote for life.

Is that really the line between who is worthy of a voice and who is not?

Democracy is not a system where only the virtuous get to participate. It is a system where everyone participates and we collectively strive toward justice. The ballot is not a medal for good character. It is a tool for shared self-governance.

Incarcerated people are part of our communities

Some say, “I can support restoring rights after people leave prison—but not while they’re inside.”

But consider this: incarceration does not erase someone’s membership in their community. People in prison are sons and daughters, mothers and fathers, neighbors and workers. They come from somewhere. In most cases, they will return.

Their children go to our schools. Their families live under the policies our elected officials enact. Their hometowns are affected by budgets, by policing, by housing laws, by education reforms. To say, “While you are incarcerated, you have no say,” is to deepen the distance between them and us, to widen the gap that makes reentry harder and recidivism more likely.

Voting is an act of investment in society. It is a tiny but meaningful way of saying: I still care what happens. I still see myself as part of this community. I still believe my voice matters.

Why would we ever want to sever that connection? Why would we not, instead, nurture it?

States and countries that allow incarcerated people to vote—like Maine and Vermont here at home, and many democracies abroad—have not crumbled. Their elections still function. Their communities still stand. What they have shown is that it is entirely possible to run a democratic system that recognizes the full humanity and civic status of people behind bars.

The myth of “public safety” through silencing

Some worry that allowing people with felony convictions to vote will somehow threaten public safety. That idea rests on a dangerous misunderstanding.

Voting is not a weapon. A ballot is not a gun. Casting a vote does not endanger neighborhoods; in many ways, it protects them.

People with lived experience of the criminal legal system know firsthand where our policies fail—where support for mental health is missing, where housing is unstable, where addiction is treated as a crime instead of a health issue, where reentry services are nonexistent. Their insights are indispensable to building safer communities.

If we want policies that reduce harm, prevent crime, and support healing, why would we silence the very people who know the system from the inside?

Study after study shows that civic engagement—having a job, being connected to community, feeling invested in collective decisions—is associated with lower recidivism. Voting is not a magic cure, but it is part of a web of belonging. It sends a message: You are still one of us, and we expect you to contribute.

That message does far more to promote safety than banishing someone into political invisibility ever could.

Answering the hard question: “What about serious crimes?”

There is another question people ask quietly: “What about murderers? What about people who have committed the most serious harm? Should they vote too?”

Yes. They should.

This is not because their crimes are unimportant. It is precisely because we insist that even the gravest act does not erase a person’s status as a human being and as a citizen.

We can—and must—hold people accountable. We can—and must—protect the public. We can impose sentences, including very long ones, when necessary. But none of that requires us to sever the political bond between a person and their society.

If the state can decide that some crimes remove your status as a voter, it can expand that category as it chooses. Yesterday it was murder. Today it is a drug offense. Tomorrow it is something else. The more we tether fundamental rights to shifting criminal codes, the more we expose all of us to the whims of power.

If citizenship means anything, it must be stronger than the worst thing a person has done.

This is not about condoning harm; it is about refusing to multiply it

Some will say: “Restoring voting rights is letting people off the hook.”

No. Accountability is about facing consequences, making amends, and working to repair harm. It is not about stripping away every shred of dignity.

Disenfranchisement does not heal victims. It does not rebuild burned bridges. It does not house the unhoused, treat trauma, or restore lost lives. It simply adds another layer of harm—this time, a harm aimed not just at the convicted person but at the entire democratic body.

True justice can center victims, build safety, and still protect the civic rights of those who caused harm. These are not competing goals. In fact, a society that models fairness and proportionality is better positioned to prevent future harm.

A simple standard: governed = represented

Let us adopt a simple principle: if the government has power over you, you must have the right to vote on that government.

If you can be arrested by the police, you should have a say in who oversees the police.
If you can be sentenced by a judge, you should have a say in who writes the laws judges enforce.
If you can be counted in the census to draw political districts—as incarcerated people are—then your voice must be counted in elections as well.

Anything less is taxation without representation. Anything less is rule over, not rule by, the people.

A call to courage and imagination

Restoring voting rights to all citizens with felony convictions—including those currently incarcerated—is not a small reform. It challenges us to rethink who “the people” truly are. It asks us to stop drawing a line between the “deserving” and “undeserving” citizen.

It forces us to confront ugly truths about race, about class, about power in this country. And it demands courage.

Legislators will tell you it’s too controversial. Pundits will say it’s politically risky. Some will insist that the public isn’t ready.

But the public can be led. Hearts can change. We live in a country where women once could not vote, where Black people were once barred openly from the ballot box, where literacy tests and poll taxes once ruled. Those who fought to end those injustices were told they were going too far, too fast.

History has judged them, and it calls them right.

This is the next chapter in that same struggle.

What we must do

We must demand laws that:

  • Automatically restore voting rights to every citizen with a felony conviction, without conditions, fees, or bureaucratic hurdles.
  • Guarantee the right to vote from prison, treating incarcerated citizens as full participants in elections.
  • End racialized practices of disenfranchisement and invest in communities that have been systematically silenced.
  • Educate and register eligible voters in jails, prisons, and all reentry programs, making the ballot accessible to all.

We must build a culture that understands: people can do harm and still deserve a voice; people can be punished and still remain part of us; people can change, and our laws should allow for that transformation.

Closing

When we deny someone the vote, we are not just saying, “You have done wrong.” We are saying, “You no longer count.” That is a sentence no human institution should ever pronounce on a citizen.

Universal suffrage means universal. Not for the perfect. Not for the privileged. Not for the unblemished. For everyone.

Let us be a country brave enough to live up to the promise we have etched into our ideals, if not yet fully into our laws: that every citizen has a voice, and that no one is forever exiled from the people.

Let us restore the vote to every citizen with a felony conviction, including those behind bars, and in doing so, bring our democracy closer to what it claims to be.

The question is not whether they are worthy of a vote. The question is whether we are worthy of calling ourselves a democracy if we deny it.

Thank you.

The Unbreakable Ballot: Why Felons, Including the Incarcerated, Must Vote

In a democracy, the right to vote is more than a privilege; it is the bedrock of citizenship, the primary mechanism by which people shape the laws that govern them. Yet across the United States, millions of citizens are denied this fundamental right solely because they have been convicted of a felony. Even after serving their sentences, many face lifelong disenfranchisement, and in some states those currently incarcerated are completely excluded from the political process. This systematic exclusion is a profound injustice that undermines the very principles of democracy, equality, and human dignity. Universal suffrage— the right of all adult citizens to vote—must be restored to every person convicted of a felony, without exception, including those still behind bars.

Voting as a Fundamental Human Right

The right to vote is enshrined in international human rights law. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 21) states that “everyone has the right to take part in the government of his country, directly or through freely chosen representatives.” The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Article 25) similarly guarantees citizens the right to vote and be elected. These instruments recognize voting as an inalienable right that cannot be suspended arbitrarily. While some rights may be lawfully restricted as a consequence of criminal conduct—such as liberty—the right to vote is not a right that should be forfeited because of a criminal conviction. It is a fundamental expression of personhood and equality before the law.

The U.S. Constitution, too, protects voting as a fundamental right. The Fifteenth, Nineteenth, and Twenty-Sixth Amendments prohibit disenfranchisement based on race, sex, and age, respectively. Though the Constitution allows states to set voting qualifications, any restriction must meet strict scrutiny. Punishing a citizen with permanent loss of voting rights after a felony conviction is a severe, blanket deprivation that bears no relationship to the legitimate goals of punishment and raises serious equal protection concerns.

Incarceration Does Not Nullify Citizenship

A felony conviction results in the loss of certain civil liberties—such as freedom of movement while incarcerated—but it does not erase a person’s citizenship. Citizens retain their status as members of the polity even while serving time. Denying them the vote implies that they have ceased to be part of the political community, which is a dangerous notion. Historically, the idea that some people are “unfit” to participate in government has been used to justify excluding women, African Americans, and the poor. Today, felon disenfranchisement serves a similar function, disproportionately affecting minorities and the economically disadvantaged, thereby reinforcing structural inequalities.

Moreover, the principle of “no taxation without representation” is violated when prisoners are counted for census purposes—affecting legislative districts—but are barred from voting. Many prisoners are required to work while incarcerated, often for meager wages, and pay taxes on any earnings. They are subject to laws made by representatives they had no say in electing. This is fundamentally un-American.

Democratic Legitimacy and Social Cohesion

A healthy democracy depends on the inclusion of all voices. When millions of people are excluded from the electoral process, policies are shaped without considering their interests, leading to laws that are less just and less effective. Including incarcerated voters would force policymakers to address issues that affect the prison population—such as sentencing reform, prison conditions, and reentry programs—thereby improving the quality of legislation and promoting social cohesion.

Additionally, voting is a powerful tool for rehabilitation. Participation in the political process can foster a sense of civic responsibility, self-worth, and connection to society. Studies have shown that former inmates who vote are less likely to reoffend, as voting reinforces social bonds and encourages lawful behavior. Extending the franchise to those currently incarcerated could therefore contribute to lower recidivism rates, benefitting both individuals and communities.

Racial Justice and the Legacy of Disenfranchisement

Felon disenfranchisement has a stark racial impact. In the United States, one in 13 African Americans is disenfranchised, compared to one in 56 non‑Black voters. This disparity is not accidental; it stems from a history of using criminal law to suppress Black political participation, from post‑Reconstruction “Black Codes” to the modern War on Drugs. By excluding felons from voting, we perpetuate a system that disproportionately silences minority voices, distorting democratic outcomes and entrenching racial inequality.

Restoring voting rights to all felons would be a crucial step toward rectifying these injustices. It would acknowledge that the criminal justice system has been weaponized against certain communities and would begin to repair the damage by re‑empowering those who have been systematically marginalized.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Argument 1: “If you break the law, you lose your rights.”
Criminal punishments already include loss of liberty, fines, and other sanctions. Adding permanent disenfranchisement is an extra penalty not required by the goals of retribution, deterrence, or rehabilitation. It is a collective punishment that extends beyond the individual’s sentence, violating the principle of proportionality.

Argument 2: “Prisoners lack the information to vote responsibly.”
This claim is unfounded. Many prisoners are highly informed about current events, and the mere fact of incarceration does not imply ignorance. Moreover, the right to vote does not depend on passing a knowledge test; such a requirement would be unconstitutional and antithetical to democratic inclusivity. If concerned, civic education programs can be provided—just as they are for the general population.

Argument 3: “Allowing prisoners to vote could manipulate election outcomes.”
There is no evidence that prisoners would vote as a monolithic bloc or that their votes would swing elections in a way that undermines democratic legitimacy. Even if they did, that would simply reflect the political preferences of a segment of the populace. In a democracy, every citizen’s voice matters equally. The fear of “undesirable” voters is a recurring excuse for disenfranchisement that has been used throughout history to exclude the powerless.

Argument 4: “Victims’ rights are violated when perpetrators vote.”
Victims have a right to see justice served, but that does not include stripping the convicted of all civil rights after they have served their sentences.justice is not about perpetual punishment; it is about accountability and restoration. Denying the vote does not restore victims; it merely continues to harm the offender and society.

Argument 5: “States should decide their own voting rules.”
While states have authority over election administration, that authority is not unlimited. The U.S. Supreme Court has repeatedly held that voting is a fundamental right and that state restrictions must be narrowly tailored to serve a compelling state interest. Blanket felon disenfranchisement fails that test. Moreover, fundamental rights should not vary from state to state based on arbitrary distinctions; they should be universally protected.

Conclusion

The right to vote is the cornerstone of democratic citizenship. It cannot be treated as a conditional reward for good behavior; it is an inherent attribute of personhood that persists even behind bars. Granting voting rights to all citizens convicted of felonies, including the incarcerated, affirms the principle that every person deserves a voice in the laws that bind them. It strengthens democracy, promotes rehabilitation, advances racial justice, and upholds the values of equality and human dignity. The time has come to end the shameful practice of felon disenfranchisement and to ensure that the ballot box is open to every citizen, without exception. Only then can we truly claim to be a government of the people, by the people, for the people.

Voting is not a privilege contingent on good behavior but a fundamental right intrinsic to citizenship. Restoring voting rights to incarcerated citizens rectifies historical injustices, reinforces rehabilitation, and affirms that no individual is beyond the reach of civic belonging. As the nation grapples with mass incarceration and racial inequality, ending felony disenfranchisement is a moral and democratic imperative. Universal suffrage must mean exactly that—universal—for in the words of Frederick Douglass, “No man can be truly free whose liberty is dependent upon the mere will of another.”

At its core, democracy rests on the principle that governments derive their legitimacy from the consent of the governed. The right to vote is not a privilege to be earned or lost, but an inherent aspect of citizenship that connects individuals to their community and affirms their fundamental humanity.

To deny them participation in the democratic process while demanding their compliance with its outcomes represents a fundamental contradiction in democratic theory. If we accept that human dignity and basic rights persist regardless of criminal behavior—which is why we prohibit cruel and unusual punishment—then we must also accept that the right to democratic participation cannot be severed by conviction alone.

The Myth of Forfeiture

Proponents of felony disenfranchisement often argue that those who violate society's laws have forfeited their right to participate in making those laws. This argument fails on multiple grounds. First, it assumes that all crimes represent an equal rejection of social contract, ignoring the vast disparities in what constitutes a felony across jurisdictions. Drug possession, tax evasion, and even some forms of protest can result in felony convictions that trigger lifelong voting bans in certain states.

More fundamentally, the forfeiture argument treats voting rights as transactional rather than inherent. We don't strip other fundamental rights based on criminal conviction—freedom of religion, protection from cruel punishment, or the right to legal representation all remain intact. The selective removal of voting rights reveals that disenfranchisement serves not as logical consequence but as additional punishment, one that extends far beyond any reasonable conception of justice or public safety.

Our criminal justice system ostensibly aims to rehabilitate offenders and prepare them for successful reintegration into society. Denying voting rights directly contradicts these goals by severing one of the most important connections between individuals and their communities. Political participation encourages civic engagement, investment in community outcomes, and adherence to social norms—exactly the behaviors we should be fostering in those who have committed crimes.

Research consistently demonstrates that civic participation, including voting, correlates with reduced recidivism rates. When people feel invested in their communities and believe they have a voice in shaping society's direction, they are more likely to become law-abiding, productive citizens. By maintaining voting rights even during incarceration, we send a powerful message that individuals remain valued members of society capable of redemption and positive contribution. The effects of felony disenfranchisement fall disproportionately on communities of color, amplifying existing racial disparities in the criminal justice system. Due to disparate policing, prosecution, and sentencing practices, Black Americans are incarcerated at nearly five times the rate of white Americans. This creates a vicious cycle where the communities most affected by criminal justice policies have the least power to change them through democratic means.

Far from protecting democracy, felony disenfranchisement undermines it by reducing the representative nature of our elections. When millions of citizens cannot participate, electoral outcomes reflect the will of only a partial population. This democratic feedback loop would strengthen, not weaken, our institutions by ensuring they remain responsive to all citizens' needs.

The path forward requires courage to challenge conventional assumptions and wisdom to recognize that our democracy grows stronger when it includes all voices, especially those who have experienced its failures most directly.

The measure of a just society lies not in how it treats its most privileged members but in how it maintains the dignity and rights of those it punishes. The Ballot Behind Bars: Why Universal Suffrage Must Mean Universal

A Defense of Voting Rights for All Citizens, Including the Incarcerated

The right to vote is not a privilege bestowed by the state upon those it deems worthy. It is the foundational mechanism through which a democratic government derives its legitimacy. When we strip that right from any citizen—including those convicted of felonies and currently serving sentences—we do not strengthen democracy. We betray it. The practice of felony disenfranchisement is a moral failure, a constitutional contradiction, and a policy rooted not in justice but in a long, ugly history of racial and class-based exclusion. It is time to end it entirely.

The Philosophical Foundation: Rights Versus Privileges

Democratic theory, from Locke to Rawlings, rests on the principle that legitimate governance requires the consent of the governed. This is not a conditional relationship. The social contract does not contain an asterisk directing citizens to fine print that reads, "unless you have committed a crime we have designated as sufficiently serious." A person convicted of a felony remains a citizen. They remain subject to taxation. They remain subject to the laws of the jurisdiction. They remain, upon release, expected to reintegrate as full participants in civic life. To deny them the most elementary tool of civic participation—the vote—while maintaining every obligation of citizenship is not justice. It is tyranny dressed in legal formalism.

Consider the logic carefully. We do not strip convicted felons of their First Amendment right to free speech. We do not strip them of their right to practice religion. We do not strip them of their protection against cruel and unusual punishment—indeed, the Eighth Amendment exists precisely to protect those who have been convicted. The right to vote, enshrined and expanded through the Fifteenth, Nineteenth, Twenty-Fourth, and Twenty-Sixth Amendments, has been treated by the American constitutional tradition as fundamental and expanding. Felony disenfranchisement is the glaring, indefensible exception to this trajectory—a place where the arc of democratic expansion reverses course and contracts.

Some argue that committing a serious crime constitutes a forfeiture of certain rights—that the social contract is bilateral, and breaking the law justifies the removal of civic standing. But this argument proves too much. If criminal behavior justifies the removal of fundamental rights, why stop at voting? Why not strip felons of the right to a fair trial in future proceedings? Why not remove their right to legal counsel? The answer, of course, is that we recognize certain rights as inalienable—not contingent on good behavior but inherent in personhood and citizenship. Voting belongs in that category. The moment we allow the state to decide which citizens deserve democratic participation, we have created a mechanism of political exclusion that is antithetical to democracy itself.

The Historical Reality: A Tool of Racial Exclusion

Felony disenfranchisement in the United States cannot be understood apart from its racial origins. While some disenfranchisement provisions existed before the Civil War, the practice expanded dramatically during the Reconstruction era, when Southern states, furious at the passage of the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, sought alternative mechanisms to suppress the Black vote. States like Mississippi, Alabama, and Virginia tailored their felony disenfranchisement laws to target offenses believed to be more commonly committed by Black citizens while excluding offenses more commonly associated with white citizens. The 1901 Alabama Constitutional Convention stated its purpose explicitly: to establish white supremacy within the bounds of federal law. Felony disenfranchisement was one of its primary tools.

This is not merely historical trivia. The effects persist with mathematical precision. Today, according to The Sentencing Project, an estimated 4.6 million Americans are disenfranchised due to felony convictions. Black Americans are disenfranchised at a rate nearly four times that of non-Black Americans. In states like Tennessee, Florida, and Mississippi, more than one in seven Black adults has lost the right to vote. This is not coincidence. It is the legacy of laws designed for exactly this purpose, operating within a criminal justice system that continues to disproportionately police, prosecute, and incarcerate Black and brown communities.

To defend felony disenfranchisement today is to defend, whether intentionally or not, a system engineered for racial exclusion. The fact that these laws are facially neutral does not cleanse them of their origins or their ongoing disparate impact. The Supreme Court itself, in Hunter v. Underwood (1985), struck down a provision of the Alabama Constitution because its original purpose was racial discrimination. Yet the broader architecture of felony disenfranchisement—built on the same foundation, in the same era, for the same reasons—remains largely intact.

The Practical Case: Better Policy, Stronger Democracy

Beyond the moral and historical arguments, the practical case for enfranchising incarcerated citizens is compelling. Opponents often raise the specter of an uninformed or malicious voting bloc—prisoners voting to weaken criminal laws or electing candidates hostile to public safety. This fear is both empirically unfounded and philosophically incoherent.

First, the numbers. The United States incarcerates approximately 1.9 million people at any given time, out of an eligible voting population of roughly 240 million. Even if every incarcerated person voted—an unlikely scenario given that voter turnout among eligible citizens rarely exceeds 60% in presidential elections—their votes would constitute less than one percent of the electorate. The idea that this population would constitute a dangerous voting bloc capable of undermining public safety is fantasy, not analysis.

Second, the premise is offensive. We do not require any other group of citizens to demonstrate that they will vote "correctly" before granting them the franchise. We do not administer ideological litmus tests at polling stations. We do not disenfranchise citizens who hold views we find abhorrent, dangerous, or ignorant. The entire premise of democracy is that the collective judgment of all citizens, regardless of their individual perspectives, produces legitimate governance. Carving out exceptions based on what we think a group might do with their votes is the logic of authoritarianism, not democracy.

Third, research consistently demonstrates that civic participation, including voting, is positively correlated with successful reentry and reduced recidivism. A landmark study by Uggen and Manza found that former offenders who voted were significantly less likely to be rearrested than those who did not. This makes intuitive sense: voting is an act of civic identity, a declaration that one belongs to and has a stake in the broader community. Disenfranchisement sends the opposite message—that the person is permanently outside the community, permanently other. If we are serious about rehabilitation and reducing recidivism, we should be encouraging civic engagement at every stage, including during incarceration, not erecting barriers to it.

The International Perspective: America as Outlier

The United States stands virtually alone among established democracies in the breadth of its felony disenfranchisement practices. Most European nations, including Germany, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, permit prisoners to vote. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in Hirst v. United Kingdom (2005) that blanket disenfranchisement of prisoners violates the right to free elections under the European Convention on Human Rights. Canada's Supreme Court, in Sauvé v. Canada (2002), struck down prisoner disenfranchisement in a decision that deserves quoting at length:

> "The right to vote is fundamental to our democracy and the rule of law and cannot be lightly set aside. Denying penitentiary inmates the right to vote is more likely to send messages that undermine respect for the law and democracy than messages that enhance those values."

Chief Justice McLachlin's reasoning is devastating in its clarity. Denying the vote does not reinforce respect for the law. It undermines it. It tells incarcerated citizens that the system that governs their lives—that determines the conditions of their confinement, the length of their sentences, the availability of rehabilitation programs, the rules of parole—is a system in which they have no voice. It tells them they are governed without consent. It recreates, in miniature, the very condition that democratic revolutions were fought to abolish.

The United States, which fashions itself as the world's leading democracy, should be embarrassed by the comparison. In Maine and Vermont, incarcerated people can vote, and the republic has not crumbled. Washington, D.C., restored voting rights to incarcerated citizens in 2020. These jurisdictions provide living proof that the fears of opponents are unfounded.

Answering the Objections

"Felons have demonstrated a disregard for the social contract." This argument assumes that the social contract is a binary—that one is either in full compliance or in total breach. But citizenship is not a contract that can be voided by misconduct. A citizen who commits a crime is punished through the mechanisms the law provides: incarceration, fines, probation, community service. These are the prescribed consequences. Adding the loss of voting rights is an extrajudicial punishment—a civil death layered on top of the criminal sentence. Moreover, this argument ignores the vast spectrum of offenses classified as felonies, from nonviolent drug possession to white-collar fraud. The idea that all felons have equally "disregarded the social contract" is a fiction that collapses under minimal scrutiny.

"Voting is a privilege that must be earned." This is the argument of every regime that has ever restricted the franchise. It was used to deny the vote to the propertyless, to women, to Black Americans, to eighteen-year-olds sent to die in Vietnam. History has judged every previous iteration of this argument as wrong. It is no less wrong when applied to the incarcerated. Voting is not a gold star for good behavior. It is the mechanism by which free people govern themselves. A government that selectively grants and revokes it based on conduct is not a democracy—it is a custodial state distributing privileges.

"Victims of crime would be offended." This appeal to the feelings of victims, while understandable, cannot be the basis for constitutional rights. Rights exist precisely to protect against majoritarian sentiment. Many victims of crime, in fact, support the restoration of voting rights, recognizing that rehabilitation and reintegration—not permanent civic death—serve their long-term interests and safety. Furthermore, many incarcerated individuals are themselves victims of crime, of systemic neglect, of poverty, and of the very policies they had no vote to influence. Their suffering does not count for less because of their legal status.

The Deeper Principle: Who Democracy Is For

At the deepest level, the question of whether incarcerated people should vote is a question about who democracy is for. Is it for the worthy? The law-abiding? The respectable? Or is it for everyone—messy, flawed, sometimes criminal, sometimes broken, but still citizens, still human, still subject to the laws that the rest of us get to shape?

Democracy is not a reward. It is a system of governance, and its legitimacy depends on inclusion. Every person excluded from the franchise is a person governed without consent, and a government that rules without the consent of the governed is, by definition, illegitimate in its exercise of power over those excluded persons. When we lock a person in a cell, determine the food they eat, the medical care they receive, the educational opportunities available to them, and the conditions of their daily existence—all through legislative and executive decisions made by elected officials—and then deny that person any voice in selecting those officials, we have created a relationship of pure domination. We have not preserved democracy. We have abandoned it, selectively, for those we have decided do not deserve it.

This is precisely what democracy was designed to prevent.

Conclusion

The disenfranchisement of citizens convicted of felonies—especially those currently incarcerated—is indefensible. It is philosophically inconsistent with democratic principles. It is historically rooted in racial animus. It is practically counterproductive to the goals of rehabilitation and public safety. It places the United States outside the consensus of the democratic world. And it perpetuates a system in which millions of disproportionately Black and brown citizens are governed without representation.

Universal suffrage must mean what it says. Not suffrage for the deserving. Not suffrage for the free. Not suffrage for those whose conduct meets the approval of the majority. Universal. Every citizen. Every election. No exceptions.

The measure of a democracy is not how it treats its most admired citizens. It is how it treats its most despised. If the franchise cannot survive contact with the prison cell, it was never truly universal, and the democracy that withholds it was never truly democratic.

It is time to let every citizen vote.

The Unfinished Promise: Why Every Citizen Deserves a Vote

Fellow citizens,

I stand before you today to talk about a promise — a promise this nation has been making, and breaking, and remaking for nearly 250 years. The promise that in a government of the people, all the people have a voice.

And at every single turn, history proved those voices wrong.

Let's start with fundamentals. We have allowed a dangerous idea to take root in our democracy — the idea that the right to vote is a reward for good behavior. That citizenship is something that can be downgraded. That the ballot is a gold star handed out to those the state deems worthy.

That is not what a right is.

A right is not a gift from the government. A right is what you possess because you are a human being and a citizen of this republic. You don't earn the First Amendment. You don't audition for the Fourth. And you should not have to prove your moral worthiness to access the most fundamental mechanism of self-governance ever devised.

"But They Broke the Social Contract"

I hear this argument constantly. "They committed a crime. They violated the social contract. Why should they get a say in the laws they refused to follow?"

Let me answer that directly.

First — a person convicted of a felony does not stop being governed. They are still subject to every law, every tax, every policy decision made by elected officials. They are still sent to wars declared by congresses they didn't choose. They still breathe air regulated — or unregulated — by agencies they had no voice in creating. If taxation without representation was tyranny in 1773, what do we call incarceration without representation in 2024?

Second — we do not strip other rights on this basis. A person convicted of a felony retains the right to free speech. They retain the right to practice their religion. They retain the right to due process if charged with another crime. We have never accepted the principle that committing a crime forfeits your entire claim to citizenship. So why do we accept it for the one right that defines citizenship in a democracy?

Third — and I want you to really sit with this — the "social contract" argument assumes the contract was fair to begin with. It assumes that every person convicted of a felony had equal access to education, to opportunity, to competent legal counsel, to a system that treated them justly regardless of their race or their zip code or the size of their bank account.

We know — we know — that is not true.

Let's Talk About Who Actually Loses This Right

Felony disenfranchisement is not colorblind. It has never been colorblind. And it was never designed to be colorblind.

After the Civil War, when the 15th Amendment threatened to bring millions of Black Americans into the electorate, states across the South — and let's be honest, not only the South — rewrote their constitutions with surgical precision. They made specific crimes — crimes stereotypically associated with Black citizens — into triggers for disenfranchisement, while leaving other crimes untouched. This is not speculation. This is the documented, stated intent of the framers of those provisions.

Today, one in sixteen Black adults is disenfranchised. In some states, it is one in five. The war on drugs, mandatory minimums, three-strikes laws, cash bail, racially biased policing — these policies funneled millions of disproportionately Black and brown Americans into a system that then stripped them of political power.

And then we wonder why those same communities can't vote their way to better schools, better healthcare, better policing. We took away the tool and then blamed them for the house not being built.

This is not a bug in the system. For much of American history, this was the system's purpose.

Now, I know this is where I lose some of you. Some of you might say, "Okay, after they've served their time, sure. But during incarceration? That goes too far."

I understand that instinct. But I want to challenge it.

A person in prison is still a citizen. They are still affected by government policy — arguably more than any free citizen. The conditions of their confinement, the quality of their food, their access to medical care, whether they will have any hope of rehabilitation or education, the very length of their sentence — all of these are determined by elected officials and the laws those officials write.

To deny incarcerated people the vote is to say that the people most directly subject to state power should have zero say in how that power is exercised. Think about what kind of incentive structure that creates. Think about what happens when millions of people are held in facilities run by a government they have no ability to hold accountable.

That is not justice. That is the definition of powerlessness.

And before anyone says this is radical — Maine and Vermont have never taken the vote from incarcerated citizens. Washington, D.C. restored it. Countries we consider fellow democracies — Canada, Germany, South Africa, Israel, much of the European Union — allow prisoners to vote. As for protecting elections — from what? From the participation of people who have experienced the justice system firsthand? From people who understand poverty, addiction, institutional failure, and the consequences of bad policy in ways most legislators never will?

We should want those perspectives in our electorate. A democracy is not weakened by including more voices. It is weakened by silencing them.

And here is what disenfranchisement actually does: It makes reintegration harder. Studies consistently show that civic participation — including voting — is associated with lower recidivism. When a person feels they are part of a community, they invest in that community. When we tell returning citizens, "You are not one of us. You don't get a voice. You are less than," we are actively undermining their pathway back.

We say we want people to reenter society. Then we lock the door from the inside.

The Moral Argument

But ultimately, this is not just a policy debate. It is a moral one.

Every single expansion of the franchise in American history was met with fear. They said working men without property couldn't be trusted with the vote. They said Black Americans weren't ready. They said women were too emotional. They said eighteen-year-olds were too immature.

Every single time, the real fear was the same: that power would have to be shared. That those in control would have to listen to people they had been comfortable ignoring.

That is what's happening now. We are comfortable ignoring people with felony convictions. They are out of sight — literally, behind walls — and out of mind. And some part of our collective conscience has decided that they deserve to be ignored. That their suffering is earned. That their silence is just.

I am asking you to reject that. I am asking you to look at the full scope of American history and recognize the pattern. Every time we have said, "These people don't deserve the vote," we have been wrong.

We have always been wrong.

A Challenge

I'll close with this.

Democracy is not a reward for the virtuous. It is not a club for the deserving. Democracy is the radical, terrifying, beautiful idea that every person subject to the authority of the state should have a say in how that authority is used.

Every person.

Not just the ones who have never stumbled. Not just the ones whose mistakes weren't criminalized. Not just the ones who could afford a good lawyer. Not just the ones whose skin color didn't make them a suspect before they ever did a thing wrong.

Everyone.

The measure of a democracy is not how it treats its most powerful citizens. It is how it treats its most marginalized. And right now, four million Americans are paying a price that no just democracy should ever extract — the price of silence. The price of invisibility. The price of being told, "You no longer count."

We can change this. We can decide, as we have decided before at every great turning point in our history, that the circle of democracy must grow wider. That the promise of "we the people" must actually mean all the people.

Not someday. Now.

Because a right that can be taken from anyone is secure for no one. And a democracy that excludes millions is not yet a democracy.

Let's finish the work. Let's make the promise real.

Thank you.
